transcript:
Header: Date/Time: 2026-11-09 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42 mins | Recording: yes
Attendees: Ethan Coleman (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood CSM), Lina Roberts (Verdant VP Eng), Marco Diaz (Verdant SRE), Sofia Alvarez (Verdant Security), Janelle Wu (Verdant Product)

Summary: quick sync to close out the escalation, review postmortem findings, confirm immediate mitigations and next steps.

00:00 Ethan Coleman: hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time, we'll keep this tight, main goals are to run through root cause, what we rolled out last week and the next steps to make sure this doesn't recur.
00:16 Lina Roberts: thanks Ethan, yeah appreciate the follow up, our execs wanted a clear list of what changed and what else you recommend. we saw that ~20% traffic spikes led to elevated latency then a cascade of KV cache misses? can you clarify that bit, i think some of the language in the doc was a little opaque.
00:29 Priya Nair: sure, so to summarize the RCA - during the incident there was a combination of a sudden tail of long sequences and an unusual hit on a small set of heavy prompt templates. that caused the in-memory KV cache to evict more aggressively than expected, which increased token generation work and pushed some worker pods over CPU thresholds. the autoscaler configured for pod cpu-based scaling didn't trigger fast enough because the CPU metrics we're using are smoothed at 60s, so we had ~2 minutes of subpar capacity before the fallback kicked in.
01:02 Marco Diaz: so the autoscale delay is the primary bottleneck, not Redwood serving runtime? are we sure the serving runtime couldn't keep up if autoscale acted faster?
01:12 Priya Nair: it's a mix — the runtime handled single requests fine, but throughput under that pattern required more instances; plus we saw some KV cache thrashing which increased per-request cost. if we had lower eviction rates (larger cache, different sharding) and a faster scaler trigger (or predictive scaling), we'd have avoided the queue buildup.
01:33 Janelle Wu: i remember seeing references to "K-V cash" in the transcription earlier which was funny but yes that was our main point.
01:41 Ethan Coleman: (laughs) yeah transcriber struggle. quick note on what we rolled out: Wednesday night we pushed a three-part mitigation — 1) emergency circuit breaker to drop extremely expensive templates (configurable), 2) route-on-degradation policy to fall back to a smaller model variant when latency crosses threshold, 3) increased our cache size and adjusted eviction policy in the cluster for Verdant's tenant. that got latency down to baseline within about 6 minutes.
02:12 Marco Diaz: can you explain route-on-degradation? is that the same as model fallback? what triggers it?
02:18 Priya Nair: it's model fallback — the policy watches p95 latency and error rate; if p95 exceeds 750ms for two consecutive 30s windows we route new requests to a compatible, smaller model that's pre-warmed. that way customers keep availability, albeit with lower quality for a small subset.
02:37 Sofia Alvarez: from a security and compliance perspective we need to know what logs were captured and how they were rotated. also KMS keys — we heard some mention of key rotation during the incident, is that related?
02:47 Ethan Coleman: good question — the key rotation was unrelated to the outage, that was a separate scheduled job that overlapped; we have since moved rotations to a maintenance window and confirmed it didn't block any decryption calls. logs: we captured request-level metrics and sanitized traces; Priya will share sanitized logs with PII removed.
03:06 Priya Nair: yes, we'll sanitize and provide a timeline. note: there were some gaps in tracing due to the ingestion pipeline dropping spans when the queue grew; we plan to buffer traces to S3 for at least 48 hours to avoid losing them in future.
03:25 Lina Roberts: buffer to S3 — ok that helps for forensics. what about alerting? our SREs didn't get paged until after execs reached out.
03:35 Priya Nair: right, current alert thresholds were too conservative; we'll add a latency-based page for p95 > 600ms sustained 60s and an autoscale lag alert when scaling events lag request growth by more than 90s. also recommend a synthetic test hitting the heavy templates every 5 minutes to detect the pattern earlier.
03:57 Marco Diaz: that synthetic test — can Redwood host it or do we run it from our side? we don't want extra noise in production.
04:04 Ethan Coleman: Redwood can host a synthetic probe from our staging and prod vantage points; we can run against a dedicated health endpoint that doesn't count against your usage. we'll share the script and you can opt-in.
04:16 Janelle Wu: how about the longer-term reliability changes, like autoscale policy? predictive scaling sounds promising.
04:22 Priya Nair: we have two tracks: 1) conservative: reduce smoothing window from 60s to 15s, tune cool-downs; 2) predictive: use request-rate signals and model queuing to forecast demand and pre-scale. predictive requires more data but we've piloted it with two customers and saw a 40% reduction in cold-start latency during spikes.
04:45 Lina Roberts: cost implications? predictive scaling sounds expensive.
04:49 Ethan Coleman: yes there's tradeoff — predictive will raise baseline cost slightly but reduces SLO violations. Redwood Optimize will provide cost/perf simulations for both options so you can choose: e.g., predictive + constrained max instances vs conservative faster scaling.
05:05 Sofia Alvarez: on compliance: can we get an export of who accessed the logs and audit trail around the changes you made? we need that for our internal audit.
05:13 Samir Patel: yes we'll provide an audit report showing config changes, who triggered the emergency policies and timestamps. also include the rollback history.
05:25 Marco Diaz: earlier you mentioned cache sharding — is that something we can change quickly?
05:29 Priya Nair: yes, we can change sharding and increase per-shard memory with a config deploy; low risk. we pushed a conservative increase during the incident; we'll propose the final config in the writeup.
05:40 Lina Roberts: ok good. about test plan — Marco will run the load test and we expect Redwood to be available for pairing if anything unexpected?
05:47 Marco Diaz: yes i'll run the test but I want Redwood on the call for the first run.
05:50 Ethan Coleman: absolutely, Priya and I will join the load test run. we'll also prepare a benchmarking script and a recommended cluster config.
06:00 Janelle Wu: any talk about legal/procurement? our procurement asked if this incident changes the SLA conversation.
06:07 Ethan Coleman: we can discuss SLA credits if baseline SLOs weren't met; Samir can follow up with procurement on potential remedies or credits. for now the action is the technical remediation and the postmortem doc.
06:19 Samir Patel: noted, i'll connect with your procurement contact and summarize options.
06:24 Lina Roberts: ok to recap — we want the sanitized logs + postmortem by 11/11, a recommended autoscale patch by 11/13, Verdant will run a staged load test by 11/18 with Redwood present, and a compliance/audit artifact by 11/15. plus a checkpoint after validation week of 11/22. sound right?
06:45 Ethan Coleman: yes exactly, i'll send calendar invites for the test and the checkpoint. any other open Qs?
06:51 Sofia Alvarez: one more: are there plans to push the route-on-degradation feature to our dedicated cluster or is that hosted-only?
06:58 Priya Nair: it's available for both hosted and dedicated; for your dedicated pool we can apply the policy at the edge router so it remains within your VPC. we'll include config snippets.
07:12 Lina Roberts: ok thanks everyone. appreciate the responsiveness.
07:16 Ethan Coleman: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts. meeting adjourned.

Post-call notes: some small transcription artifacts present (product names sometimes garbled). overall duration aligns ~42 minutes. action items and next steps captured and added to CRM.
